triage.name: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
triage.reason: Premature infant who remains oxygen-dependent weeks after birth; a chronic neonatal lung disease diagnosed from the clinical course and imaging, though less of a single-visit puzzle.

age.peak: first weeks to months of life in very preterm infants

demographics: Occurs almost exclusively in infants born prematurely, most often before 32 weeks' gestation
Risk rises with lower birth weight and lower gestational age
More common in infants who required prolonged oxygen or mechanical ventilation after birth

risk_factors.text: Prolonged mechanical ventilation or supplemental oxygen after birth
Chorioamnionitis or maternal infection during pregnancy

comorbidities: Respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn
social_history: Prolonged neonatal intensive care unit stay
Home oxygen and feeding support after discharge
exposures: Postnatal mechanical ventilation and supplemental oxygen

chief_complaints.text: My baby still needs oxygen and breathes fast
My baby gets tired and turns blue during feeds
My baby is not gaining weight well

hpi.onset: Insidious, developing over the first weeks to months after a premature birth; the infant remains oxygen-dependent beyond the first few days of life
hpi.duration: Weeks to months; by definition the oxygen requirement persists at 28 days of life or beyond 36 weeks' postmenstrual age
hpi.progression: Initial neonatal respiratory distress improves, but the infant cannot be weaned from oxygen or respiratory support; tachypnea, retractions and feeding difficulty persist or worsen over weeks
hpi.quality: Fast, labored breathing with intermittent wheeze and cough
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; some infants need only low-flow oxygen, others remain on mechanical ventilation or CPAP
hpi.timing: Continuous, worse with feeding, crying and activity

associated_symptoms.text: Pulling in of the chest wall with breathing
Tires easily and takes small feeds
Bluish color around the lips or face during feeds or crying

pertinent_negatives: Fever or signs of acute infection at presentation
Sudden onset of severe respiratory distress
Vomiting that is bilious or projectile

negatives: Poor feeding at baseline before this illness

atypical.how_it_differs: The youngest and most premature infants may show only oxygen dependency and poor feeding without obvious retractions or wheeze; the diagnosis is often made from the ongoing need for respiratory support rather than a distinct symptom.
Older children who had bronchopulmonary dysplasia as infants may present with recurrent wheeze, exercise intolerance and asthma-like symptoms rather than overt oxygen dependency.

general.mild: Alert, comfortable at rest on low-flow oxygen; mild tachypnea with handling
general.moderate: Tachypneic and mildly distressed, mild retractions, tires with feeds
general.severe: Ill-appearing, marked tachypnea and retractions, nasal flaring, needs substantial respiratory support
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, exhausted or lethargic, grunting, cyanotic, may need escalation of ventilatory support

findings.maneuver: Observe the infant's respiratory rate over a full minute while calm
findings.finding: Sustained respiratory rate above the normal range for age

findings.maneuver: Observe the infant's oxygen saturation on room air or note the supplemental oxygen requirement
findings.finding: Desaturation when oxygen is reduced or weaned, requiring continued supplemental oxygen

findings.maneuver: Inspect the chest wall during quiet breathing
findings.finding: Intercostal and subcostal indrawing with inspiration
Flaring of the alae nasi with each breath

findings.maneuver: Auscultate over the mouth and chest during breathing
findings.finding: Expiratory grunting

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the lung fields with a small-bore stethoscope
findings.finding: Fine inspiratory crackles, often basal

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the lung fields during expiration
findings.finding: Expiratory wheeze

findings.maneuver: Auscultate and time the expiratory phase
findings.finding: Expiratory phase longer than inspiratory phase

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, tongue and nail beds during feeding or crying
findings.finding: Central or perioral bluish discoloration

findings.maneuver: Plot weight, length and head circumference on the growth chart and compare with prior measurements
findings.finding: Weight below expected for age or crossing down on the growth curve

findings.maneuver: Observe a feed and ask the caregiver about stamina and volume taken
findings.finding: Tires during feeds, takes small volumes, desaturates while feeding

findings.maneuver: Inspect the chest shape from the side
findings.finding: Increased anteroposterior chest diameter
Heart murmur

findings.maneuver: Palpate the right upper quadrant and liver edge
findings.finding: Liver edge palpable below the costal margin

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for distension, tenderness and masses
findings.finding: Soft, non-distended abdomen without tenderness or mass

findings.maneuver: Assess tone, activity and the anterior fontanelle
findings.finding: Normal tone and activity, flat fontanelle

labs.caveat: Respiratory acidosis from CO2 retention in severe disease; often measured on capillary or arterial blood gas.
Elevated in infants with chronic CO2 retention; a rising value signals worsening respiratory failure.
Low on room air; the infant's oxygen requirement is the more useful bedside measure.
Compensatory metabolic alkalosis from chronic CO2 retention.
Anemia of prematurity and repeated phlebotomy; worsens oxygen delivery.
Mild elevation can reflect chronic inflammation or an intercurrent infection; a normal count does not exclude infection.
Nonspecific; helps when an acute infection is suspected.

findings.finding: Right axis deviation, normal for a neonate
Sinus tachycardia
Right ventricular dominance pattern (tall R waves in V1, deep S in V6), normal for age
Peaked P waves suggesting right atrial enlargement
Right bundle branch block pattern

findings.text: Hyperinflation with increased lung volumes and flattened diaphragms
Diffuse bilateral hazy or streaky opacities

imaging.preferred_when: When pulmonary hypertension or congenital heart disease is suspected
Rarely needed; only when another process such as a congenital lung malformation is suspected

initial.why: Assesses oxygenation and CO2 retention in an infant who cannot be weaned from oxygen
initial.only_if: respiratory failure, CO2 retention or worsening distress is suspected

initial.why: Looks for anemia of prematurity and for leukocytosis suggesting infection
Electrolytes and acid-base status in an infant on diuretics or with chronic CO2 retention
Shows hyperinflation and streaky opacities and helps exclude other causes of chronic respiratory failure
initial.only_if: Shows hyperinflation and streaky opacities and helps exclude other causes of chronic respiratory failure

supporting.why: Screens for pulmonary hypertension and congenital heart disease
supporting.only_if: a murmur, cyanosis or suspected pulmonary hypertension is present

supporting.why: Helps when an acute infection is suspected
supporting.only_if: fever or worsening respiratory status suggests infection

supporting.why: May support a bacterial infection when the picture is unclear

not_indicated.why: Not needed for routine diagnosis; reserved for atypical features suggesting another lung malformation
No role in neonatal chronic lung disease
Not part of the evaluation unless cardiac ischemia is suspected, which is not typical here

decision_points: Diagnosis is clinical: an infant born prematurely who still needs supplemental oxygen at 28 days of life or at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age
Echocardiogram before assuming the oxygen requirement is purely pulmonary, to exclude congenital heart disease and assess for pulmonary hypertension
Escalate respiratory support and evaluate for infection when CO2 rises or oxygen needs increase

criteria.name: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
criteria.summary: A chronic lung disease of preterm infants defined by an ongoing need for supplemental oxygen or respiratory support at 28 days of life or at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age, with severity graded by the amount of oxygen or ventilatory support required at that time.

differential.name: Respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn
differential.why_considered: A preterm infant with tachypnea, retractions and an oxygen requirement in the first days of life
differential.trigger: Respiratory distress in a preterm infant in the first hours to days of life

history: Distress begins within hours of birth, not weeks later
Respiratory support needs typically improve over the first week rather than persist
exam: Grunting, retractions and nasal flaring in the first hours of life
Distress that lessens as surfactant is given and the infant matures
labs: Respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia early on
Blood gas abnormalities resolve as the infant improves
imaging: Diffuse ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms and low lung volumes
Findings improve on serial films rather than showing hyperinflation with streaky opacities

differential.name: Neonatal pneumonia or sepsis
differential.why_considered: A preterm infant with respiratory distress, oxygen requirement and poor feeding
differential.trigger: Fever, temperature instability, lethargy or a sudden worsening of respiratory status

history: Maternal fever, chorioamnionitis or prolonged rupture of membranes
Acute onset or abrupt deterioration rather than a chronic stable course
Risk factors for early-onset or late-onset sepsis
exam: Temperature instability, lethargy or poor perfusion
Respiratory distress that is acute and progressive
labs: Leukocytosis or leukopenia with a left shift
imaging: Focal or diffuse opacities that change with treatment

differential.name: Congenital heart disease
differential.why_considered: An infant with cyanosis, tachypnea, poor feeding and poor weight gain
differential.trigger: A murmur, persistent cyanosis or cyanosis that does not correct with oxygen

history: Cyanosis present from birth or with feeds
Failure to thrive despite adequate oxygen
Family history of congenital heart disease
exam: Cyanosis that does not improve with supplemental oxygen
labs: Hypoxemia that is refractory to oxygen
Metabolic acidosis if low cardiac output
imaging: Abnormal cardiac silhouette or pulmonary vascularity on chest x-ray
Structural defect and abnormal flow on echocardiogram
ecg: Abnormal axis or chamber enlargement for age
Findings that do not fit the expected neonatal pattern

differential.name: Congenital lung malformation
differential.why_considered: An infant with chronic respiratory symptoms and abnormal chest imaging

history: Symptoms present from birth without a clear link to prematurity or ventilation
Recurrent infections in the same lobe
imaging: A discrete cystic or solid lesion rather than diffuse bilateral changes
CT shows a focal malformation such as a congenital pulmonary airway malformation

differential.name: Tracheobronchomalacia
differential.why_considered: An infant with noisy breathing, wheeze and difficulty weaning from respiratory support

history: Worsening of symptoms with feeding, crying or position changes
exam: Symptoms that improve with positioning or CPAP
imaging: Dynamic airway collapse on bronchoscopy or dynamic imaging
Chest x-ray may be normal or show hyperinflation

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: An infant with spitting up, feeding difficulty and respiratory symptoms

history: Spitting up and irritability with feeds
Respiratory symptoms that improve when reflux is treated
imaging: Chest x-ray without the chronic hyperinflation and streaky opacities of bronchopulmonary dysplasia

severity.mild: Infant breathing room air or needing only low-flow oxygen at 28 days of life or at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age; feeding and growth are near normal.
severity.moderate: Infant still needing supplemental oxygen or nasal CPAP at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age; tachypnea, retractions and feeding difficulty are present.
severity.severe: Infant needing invasive mechanical ventilation or high levels of respiratory support at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age; marked distress, poor growth and possible pulmonary hypertension.
severity.critical: Respiratory failure with worsening hypoxemia or CO2 retention, or pulmonary hypertension with cor pulmonale, requiring escalation of ventilatory support.

red_flags.finding: Sudden worsening of respiratory distress or a new oxygen requirement
red_flags.meaning: Suggests an acute complication such as pneumothorax, pneumonia or sepsis

red_flags.finding: Cyanosis that does not improve with supplemental oxygen
red_flags.meaning: Suggests pulmonary hypertension, a right-to-left shunt or congenital heart disease

red_flags.finding: Rising CO2 or respiratory acidosis on blood gas
red_flags.meaning: Worsening respiratory failure; may need escalation of ventilatory support

red_flags.finding: Lethargy, temperature instability or poor perfusion
red_flags.meaning: Suggests sepsis or another acute illness

red_flags.finding: Poor weight gain or falling off the growth curve
red_flags.meaning: Inadequate nutrition and increased metabolic demand; worsens lung healing and development

complications.name: Pulmonary hypertension
clues: Loud or single second heart sound

special_populations.differences: The diagnosis is defined in this group; severity is graded by the amount of oxygen or respiratory support needed at 28 days of life or at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age.
Older children who had bronchopulmonary dysplasia as infants may present with recurrent wheeze, exercise intolerance and asthma-like symptoms rather than overt oxygen dependency.

key_questions.question: How early was your baby born, and what was the birth weight?
key_questions.looking_for: Prematurity, especially before 32 weeks' gestation, and very low birth weight under 1500 g; the strongest risk factors

key_questions.question: Did your baby need oxygen or a breathing machine after birth, and for how long?
key_questions.looking_for: Prolonged mechanical ventilation or supplemental oxygen after birth, which is central to the diagnosis

key_questions.question: Is your baby still needing oxygen now, and how much?
key_questions.looking_for: Ongoing oxygen dependence at 28 days of life or at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age; the defining feature

key_questions.question: How fast is your baby breathing, and does the chest pull in with each breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Persistent tachypnea and retractions that do not resolve as expected after birth

key_questions.question: Does your baby tire or turn blue during feeds?
key_questions.looking_for: Feeding difficulty with desaturation or cyanosis, suggesting significant lung disease

key_questions.question: How is your baby's weight gain?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor weight gain or falling off the growth curve from increased work of breathing and feeding difficulty

key_questions.question: Does your baby wheeze or cough?
key_questions.looking_for: Wheeze and cough, which are common but not universal

key_questions.question: Was there any infection during the pregnancy, such as chorioamnionitis?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal infection or chorioamnionitis, a moderate risk factor

key_questions.question: Has your baby had any fever, lethargy or sudden worsening of breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: Acute infection, sepsis or pneumothorax rather than the chronic course of bronchopulmonary dysplasia

key_questions.question: Has your baby been diagnosed with a heart problem or a patent ductus arteriosus?
key_questions.looking_for: Patent ductus arteriosus or congenital heart disease, which can mimic or complicate the picture

key_questions.question: Has your baby had any bleeding in the brain or other problems of prematurity?
key_questions.looking_for: Intraventricular hemorrhage or other comorbidities of prematurity

key_questions.question: Does anyone in the family have lung or heart disease in infancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of congenital heart disease or inherited lung disease

reasoning_points: Infant born prematurely, most often before 32 weeks' gestation and with very low birth weight
Required prolonged supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation after birth
Remains oxygen-dependent at 28 days of life or at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age
Persistent tachypnea, retractions and feeding difficulty rather than a resolving neonatal course
Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation with streaky or hazy bilateral opacities
Other causes of chronic respiratory failure excluded, including congenital heart disease and infection
Severity graded by the amount of oxygen or respiratory support needed at the diagnostic time point

easy: Very preterm infant with a clear history of prolonged ventilation and oxygen
Still oxygen-dependent at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age
Classic chest x-ray with hyperinflation and streaky opacities
Tachypnea and retractions with poor weight gain
medium: Infant with mild disease who needs only low-flow oxygen and has few exam findings
Coexisting patent ductus arteriosus or suspected pulmonary hypertension
Feeding difficulty and poor growth as the main concern rather than overt distress
hard: Infant with cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen, raising concern for congenital heart disease
Sudden deterioration suggesting pneumonia, sepsis or pneumothorax rather than chronic disease
Older child with recurrent wheeze and exercise intolerance but no current oxygen requirement
Atypical imaging suggesting a congenital lung malformation
